## 1. The one who shouts  (`#the-one-who-shouts`)

Cited ayat: 2:171

> **2:171** وَمَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِى يَنْعِقُ بِمَا لَا يَسْمَعُ إِلَّا دُعَآءً وَنِدَآءً صُمٌّۢ بُكْمٌ عُمْىٌ فَهُمْ لَا يَعْقِلُونَ

### Claims

**c1** (2:171): The ayah says that the similitude of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts at what hears nothing but a call and a cry.

**c2** (2:171): They are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason.

### One-minute summary

The ayah gives the similitude of those who disbelieve as one who shouts at what hears nothing but a call and a cry [c1]. It adds that they are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason [c2].

### Complete story

The ayah says that the similitude of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts at what hears nothing but a call and a cry [c1]. They are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason [c2].

### Deep study

The ayah gives the similitude in one sentence and then states how those who disbelieve are described [c1][c2]. What hears is described only by what it hears, a call and a cry, and the ayah does not name it [c1].

### Kids mode

The ayah gives a picture of one who shouts at something that hears only a call and a cry [c1]. It says that those who disbelieve are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason [c2].

### Life lessons (educational interpretation)

Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture is about hearing a sound without understanding its meaning [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah links not using reason with being deaf, dumb and blind [c2].

### What the sources do not establish

- Not established: what is shouted at, since the ayah names it only as what hears nothing but a call and a cry.
- Not established: whether those who disbelieve are likened to the one who shouts or to what is shouted at; the comparison is read in both ways, and this draft keeps the ayah's own wording.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal).
- The Arabic word for reason (yaqilun) is rendered 'use reason'; a scholar may prefer another wording.
